Something I don’t quite know, maybe someone closer to math can answer this question
It seems we’re making tremendous progress on the back of existing abstractions and concepts with the brute force ability to generate language and verify proofs.
For example, Tao says about the Riemann proof:
> appears to use the full power of modern developments on the Langlands program and arithmetic geometry
What I wonder: how do we create new abstractions and concepts? Like whatever “Langlands program” is? That then feedback into the system, and allow for even more sophisticated mathematics.
Are we assuming AI will do this? Or does this still need to be something at least agreed-upon by a mathematics community - in the same way programmers talk about a “linked list” without having an hour long conversation to define it axiomatically? And without that social aspect, without breaking down long proofs into Lego block common abstractions, math may plateau? In part because we lose the ability to ask meaningful questions?

comments.author: seanhunter
comments.text:
I think this idea is often misunderstood and used as an excuse by people who don’t want to make any effort to understand a complex concept and want to blame the results of their laziness on the explanation or the explainer.
There are things where you may be given an explanation in simple terms, but the concept requires effort on the part of the recipient of the explanation to really understand.  I’ll give an example: compactness.  Probably anyone who has done analysis is familiar with how this concept is usually taught. Typically how it goes is you do open and closed sets and then they hit you with “a set is compact if and only if every open cover has a finite subcover”.  Now this definition is
extremely
profound but very dense and it’s highly non-obvious why that in particular is the property you want (a finite subcover for every open cover)[1], how you could go about proving that every possible open cover in a certain situation could have a finite subcover etc etc.
In this case it’s actually quite easy to give simple explanations of the separate parts of the definition (open and closed sets, what an open cover therefore means, what a finite subcover then is etc) but actually unde

comments.author: mr_mitm
comments.text:
The article is just a bunch of quotes from Richard Feynman and John Gruber. There is little insight and I even think the article is misrepresenting the quotes.
Feynman said "if you can't explain it
on a freshmen level
". Leaving out that qualifier distorts the statement.
The other quote about the magnets is also overly reductive. Saying "I don't understand it in terms you're more familiar with" is not an admission that scientists as a group don't understand it at all.
You could go into what it means to understand something, but unfortunately the article isn't doing that.

comments.author: tgv
comments.text:
Explain to what level? E.g some topics common here. How do you explain NP in simple terms? "Things that are hard to compute?" That's simple, but not much of an explanation. It leaves the listener with a practically useless definition. And how do you explain even something practical as Heartbleed or Rowhammer? Etc.
And then there's another barrier, of course: the audience. You may use simple terms, and tell a lengthy story, but some things are hard to understand. Relativity and Monty Hall come to mind. They can be explained in simple terms, but how many people get them? Probably just the ones that also understand a detailed explanation.

comments.author: keeda
comments.text:
Whenever I see this I think to myself, “I can explain something in simple terms, but it will take more time than you have.”
Or in other words, “simple” does not imply ”short.”
However I’ve seen a lack of appreciation of this distinction play out in some exec meetings where “clarity” is prioritized above nuance. There is definitely great skill involved in crafting a message for an audience, and it’s critical to internalize that execs care about different things than you. But a minimum level of shared context is required before a discussion can fit into a 30 minute meeting. That’s why Feynman’s quote mentions “freshman level.”
I understand that execs deal with an avalanche of information and uncertainty, so clarity is a highly precious commodity. But I get the sense that “clarity” often means “just give me a simple answer”, which glosses over opportunities hidden in the nuance.

comments.author: Frost1x
comments.text:
I don’t think this is true because it makes an assumption that reductionism is always possible, you can always distill every increasingly complexity into something less and less complex and maintain the overall behavior. I don’t think complexity is always reducible because sometimes the detailed nuance is absolutely critical to the distinction.
You may be able to take core ideas from something and distill them but when you have multiple interacting core ideas you may not necessarily be able to reduce them to simple terms. And almost always when you do there’s a big asterisk that the analogy has a lot of flaws.

Being able to break things down into simple explanations (maybe many of them though?) is a sign of rigorous thinking. Not being able to do so (which seems common in some fields) is a sign of the opposite.

Counterpoint by another famed physicist, Feynman:

comments.author: kodebach
comments.text:
IMO understanding and explaining are two very different skills. I understand many topics, but I'm bad at explaining most of them, simply because I'm not good at explaining things, even mundane trivial things.
If your working as a teacher or professor like Feynman, then understanding and explaining may be equatable. In such a profession you are very practiced at explaining things and explaining something you understand should be easy.
However, the "in simple terms" part also makes a crucial difference for explaining. "Simple" for what audience? Simple mean very different things for a five year old, a college freshman and something completely different again for a tradesperson.
To explain things in simple terms you don't just need to understand the concept your explaining, you also have to understand what your audience already knows and understands and you must understand those concepts yourself too.
I think the real skill in explaining is recognising and utilising this overlap between your knowledge and your audience's.

stories.title_en: The G1 Garbage Collector

comments.author: brunoborges
comments.text:
Lots of details that teams miss when tuning the JVM on Kubernetes:
1. Default heap size varies: it can be 50% of the available memory for any amount of available memory up to 256mb; ~128mb for anywhere between 256 and 512; and then 25% for anything above 512mb;
2. The JVM will still do parallel threads even when CPU limit is 1,000 or below , which triggers CPU throttling much faster. Threads such as GC (even when it is SerialGC), ForkJoin pools, Database connection pools, HTTP server, and so on.
3. The JVM behaves MUCH better with 2,000 or more milicores, and a well sized heap. Having very small containers and dozens of replicas is worse than having slightly bigger containers (cpu/memory limits) and fewer replicas, even with a different ratio (e.g. 6 replicas will perform worse than 3 replicas, even when aggregated CPU and memory limits are the same).
I've been advocating on this for years [1].
[1]
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wApqCjHWF8Q

I already have one of these but it only accepts CF/SD and other non-floppy media .. its pretty great, you pop your card in, press a button and the contents are copied directly to disk, which is then accessible via WiFi .. its a no-name brand and I’ve used it so much over the years the labels have worn off ..

comments.author: netsharc
comments.text:
I went on a backpacking tour. My aim was to take a lot of pictures, but I didn't want to carry a laptop. So my SD card backup setup was: a Raspberry Pi clone, a card reader, a 500G Sandisk USB3 external NVMe disk the size of a credit card and the thickness of maybe 3 credit cards and a power bank.
The backup routine was:
1. Plug the card to the card reader, plug it into one of the USB3 ports of the Pi.
2. Plug the NVMe disk into another USB3 port.
3. Power the contraption from my USB powerbank.
4. Plug the phone to the Pi on another USB port. Enable network sharing over USB.
5. Connect Bluetooth keyboard to the phone.
6. Open a terminal on the phone,
7. Find out the IP address of the Pi that the phone's DHCP server gave
8. SSH into the Pi.
9. Run rsync to copy files from the SD card to the NVMe disk (luckily the Linux distro auto-mounts the USB storage devices).
After all that's done I can plug the NVMe disk straight to my phone to browse the images...
I've been thinking of creating a Pi distro that creates a WiFi network, and use a Jenkins-like web UI so I can just plug everything in and control the procedure from the phone's browser. One day..!
